PROPOSED AMENDMENT RELIEVING MEMBER OF OBLIGATION TO VOTE
speechtext:
I
desire to give notice to the house that on Tuesday next I shall move that the standing orders of this house be amended by inserting the following as 9 (a):
Upon a division a member is not obliged to vote.
I have given a copy of the notice to the Clerk.

I
notice in the Hansard of yesterday that I am reported as having mentioned the name of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill; as one of those who refrained from voting on the amendment. This was an error. The hon. gentleman voted, and I think it is only fair to him that I should make this explanation.

Last evening when the vote was being taken there was what we may term an unfortunate occurrence, and some reflection was cast upon members in this corner of the house during the proceedings. I made the statement last evening that members in this corner who sat in the house while the vote on the amendment was being taken did so because of rulings of the former Speaker, the Hon. Mr. Lemieux. I am going to take the opportunity this afternoon to place upon Hansard the rulings upon which we based our action last evening.

If the hon. member for Acadia wishes to make an explanation of his vote or with regard to something that was imputed to him, that would properly be a question of privilege, but to quote at this stage precedents as to the correctness or incorrectness of the Speaker's ruling is going beyond a question of privilege.

I am not questioning your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I accept it, and very heartily. I am simply giving the reasons for my conduct last evening, and for that purpose I desire to place on record the rulings of the former Speaker.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but the hon. gentleman is out of order. The opportunity was afforded last evening very distinctly and very generously by Your Honour for hon. members to make any statements which they might desire to make. In view also of the notice of motion which has just been given by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), it is perfectly obvious that an ample opportunity will be afforded to the hon. gentleman to make any statement he desires in that connection.

I understand that the hon. member for Acadia now wishes to quote authorities to explain why his conduct was as it was last evening. If I am correct in my surmise, that is not a question of privilege, and I must rule that he is out of order.

Then may I call the attention of Your Honour to what I would call the scurrilous attack of a certain newspaper on certain members in this corner of the house because of the proceedings in the house last evening. Is that sufficient to be a question of privilege?
Privilege-Miss Macphuil

The attitude of the hon. members referred to as comprising the group in that corner of the house was thoroughly explained last evening. The hon. member for Labelle, for instance, has said that there were plenty -of precedents for what was done last night in the rulings of the former Speaker. All that the hon. member for Acadia is seeking to do now is to repeat that statement and possibly quote from the rulings or give the page numbers where they are to be found in Hansard. I submit that that is not a question of privilege.
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I can assure the house that at the first opportunity I shall put on Hansard the ruling of the former Speaker.
I shall be very glad indeed if the hon. member will avail himself of the first proper opportunity to do so.
In the Ottawa Citizen of this morning there is an article by Mr. Charles Bishop, whom I think one might fairly call the czar of the press gallery.
Oh, oh.

Perhaps I should have said the prime minister of the press gallery. In this article, discussing the vote of last night, and speaking of our group, he says:
They fell back on some precedent that a former Speaker who was a very indulgent man had created when he allowed certain members not to vote.
In case Mr. Bishop does not know the name of the former Speaker, it was the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux. He goes on to say that he is no authority on the rules that I shall read in a moment. He also says that we-
-withdrew amid a noisy demonstration. The galleries could not make out exactly whether it was with cheers or jeers. They came back when the vote was announced.
He concludes this very elevating article with the following paragraph:
At the end of the day, members filed out into the lobbies discussing the exhilarating episodes of the sitting-the speech of the Prime Minister and the return back-fire, but perhaps even more this most peculiar exhibition of abstention from voting.
It was considered the more remarkable as being that of supposedly fearless people

ordinarily most assertive in their own opinions, and some of whom are inclined to be contemptuous of other opinions.
If that includes Mr. Bishop's, I plead guilty. He goes on:
While it was condoned in a spirit of tolerance and perhaps excusable on grounds of a precedent justified by no authority on parliamentary usage, it seemed to the onlookers on the floor and in the galleries to suggest certain symptoms of spinal or intestinal deficiency.
I would like to know if Mr. Bishop is a special judge of integrity, that is if the parts of the anatomy to which he referred! have anything to do with integrity. Does the fact that he writes for Conservative, Liberal and Independent papers at the same time require a peculiar brand of integrity?
You ought to know; you do it.

I say to hon. members that the report which appeared in the paper this morning is obviously unfair. To have voted for the amendment required no courage. The amendment itself was negatived; our amendment was a substitute and we took our position of abstention because it was the logical position to take. The question of courage did not enter into the matter at all, except that it required more courage not to vote than it did to vote. Any hon. member who does not think that is so ought to try it some time. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, who yesterday got themselves very much excited about the dignity of this house-
Order, order.
That is so. I say it, and I do not take it back.
It takes a woman to have courage.

Here is a case where the dignity of parliament is being reflected upon by a member of the press gallery who enjoys the privileges of the house. I think if the representatives of the press are granted privileges they should shoulder the responsibilities which go with them. They should use decent language and be fair, or at least make some attempt to be fair to hon. members in the house. Having spent ten years in the House of Commons I care very little what the newspapers say, but this report by Mr. Bishop

Privilege-Mr. Howard
seemed to me to be going too far. I deeply resent it, and I have risen, to say so. Courage is not the thing which this Independent group lack. It might be said that to a far greater extent members of the two older parties lack that quality.
Order.
It cannot be said of us, however. It may be said that we are foolish and do not stand for the right thing, but we have courage.
On the orders of the day.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. My attention has been drawn to an item which appears on page 687 of Hansard. I refer to a remark made by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) wherein he said that I had misquoted him. I would like to say to the right hon. gentleman that at no time did I intentionally misquote him. I was referring to the question of unemployment insurance, but I was not qualifying it as either contributory or nonr-contributory. I shall be pleased to insert the word "non-contributorv" before those remarks. I regret that my right hon. friend imputed to me any motive such as expressed on that page of Hansard.
On page 679 of Hansard the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr, Hackett) referring to myself, is reported as having said:
He is the kind of Liberal who enjoys protection and wanted and got it for the industries in which he has invested his money.
I say that is not so, Mr. Speaker. I have never asked for protection of any kind, nor has protection ever been granted to me.

1.	What regulation has the government made with, regard to assistance in transportation of pure-bred or grade dairy stock to western Canada ?
2.	Has the government initiated any policy with regard to credit assistance for the purchase of dairy cattle for the western farmer?
3.	If so, what is the policy?
Mr. WEIR (Melfort).
1.	The regulations in question are as follows :
With a view to assisting farmers in western Canada to establish themselves in the breeding of cattle, and to encourage the establishment of breeding centres of approved or certified pure-bred stock for either beef or dairy purposes, the Honourable Robert Weir, Minister of Agriculture, has authorized payment by the Dominion Live Stock branch of freight charges on a limited number of carload shipments of cattle purchased from breeders and farmers within the Dominion and shipped as follows:	From any point of loading in the

Questions
Dominion of Canada, including points in the prairie provinces, to any railway point in the prairie provinces, and subject to the following conditions:-
(1)	A shipment may consist of one or more carloads of cattle purchased at one time, but not more than one shipment may be made by the same purchaser in any one calendar year.
(2)	Each carload shall contain at least twelve head of mature females or an equivalent weight in the case of younger cattle. Only cattle over eight months and not over sis years of age may be included.
(3)	All cattle must conform to the following health requirements:-
(a)	Must be from herds that have passed at least two consecutive clean tuberculin tests under the supervision of the Health of Animals branch Department of Agriculture.
(b)	Must be purchased subject to the blood test for infectious abortion (Bangs disease) if they have not already been subject to this test in the owner's herd, and declared negative.
(4)	All selections must be approved by an officer or representative of the Department of Agriculture, as to type and quality.
(5)	Each animal of dairy or of dual purpose breeding included in a shipment must be of merit from a production standpoint, recognizable under at least one of the following qualifications:-
(a)	Qualified herself in the record of performance.
(b)	Out of a dam qualified in the record of performance.
(c)	Sired by an advanced registry, selective registry or record of performance bull.
(d)	Sired by a bull out of a cow qualified in the record of performance.
(6)	A purchase may be made by a bona-fide farmer-purchaser from the prairie provinces on his own behalf, or on behalf of himself and other farmers in his own district, either directly from farmers or breeders who are owners of suitable cattle, or indirectly through or with the assistance of the properly accredited field or extension services of the various breed associations in the province where the purchase is made.
(7)	For each animal purchased, the purchaser or his representative shall forward to the Live Stock Branch, Ottawa, on forms supplied for this purpose, a declaration covering the following information:-
(a)	The breed, date of birth, registered name and number of animals.
(b)	The purchase price of the animal.
(c)	The name and address of the purchaser to whom transfer of ownership is to be made.
(8)	The Dominion Live Stock branch will assume no financial obligations other than in connection with freight charges or other transportation charges (see clause 9), and in all cases settlement or accepted arrangements therefor will be required to be made as between purchaser and vendor before shipment is made.
(9)	In addition to freight charges, the Dominion Live Stock branch will be responsible for other transportation expenses incurred in securing shipments made under this policy, as follows:-
(a)	Where the purchaser personally selects a shipment of a carload or more of cattle and supervises the transportation of same to destination, he will be allowed towards his expenses an amount equivalent to the cost of a continuous single trip railway fare from point of loading to destination point.
(b)	Where purchases are made through the other channels stated in clause 6, and an attendant is required to accompany and attend the stock to destination, the Dominion Live Stock branch will furnish such attendant, if required, providing that the purchaser will agree to pay the attendant a wage of S4 per diem for the round trip and to supply him with a continuous single trip railway ticket back to the final point of loading, and a refund will be made to the purchaser of the cost of such railway ticket on presentation of receipt secured from the railway agent for the purchase of the ticket.
(10)	As shipments of only pure-bred cattle are eligible the purchaser must obtain from the seller, with respect to each animal, a shipping voucher such as may be. detached from the registration certificate of such animal. These vouchers when properly filled in and presented to the railway agent at the time and place of making shipment will entitle the shipment to be carried at the reduced freight rates applicable to pure-bred cattle. The reduced rates, as applied to carload shipments carried in standard live stock cars, or standard box cars, will apply on all shipments made under this policy.
(11)	To secure refund of freight charges or railway fares, as described, and as available under this policy, the consignee of consignees must forward to the Chief, Cattle Division, Live Stock branch, Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, the following:-
(a)	Receipted freight bill (See clause 10).
(b)	Receipt for railway ticket purchase where the services of an attendant are involved (See clause 9-b).

Questions

(c)	Signed declaration covering complete shipment (See clause 7).
Intending purchasers of cattle under this policy are requested to familiarize themselves with the provisions as set forth. Further information in regard to the policy and the forms referred to in clause 11 may be obtained on application to the chief, cattle division, Live Stock branch, Department of Agriculture, Ottawa.

Why does the Civil Service Commission require that the employees of the Department of Agriculture, especially the stenographers, be bilinguists, in province of Quebec, while this is not required in the other provinces?

The Civil Service Commission is not requested to supply bilingual employees unless the employee would likely be required to perform work requiring a knowledge of both languages. Most of the correspondence with the headquarters office at Ottawa has to be conducted in the English language, while naturally, a great deal of correspondence with residents in Quebec, and in some districts of other provinces has to be in French. Stenographers, therefore, are generally required to possess a working knowledge, at least, of both official languages wherever such knowledge is necessary in order that they may be of maximum value to the Department by which they are employed.

1.	What success has been met with in seeding down with grass or sweet clover, weedy land at the Swift Current experimental farm; (a) with a nurse crop, (b) without a nurse
crop?	.
2.	What class of grass seed and what variety of sweet clover seem to thrive and stand the winter best at this experimental farm, having regard also to the quality of the fodder obtained therefrom?

1.	Seeding down grass or sweet clover with a nurse crop on rented, weedy land has not been successful at Swift Current.
No trials were made in seeding without a nurse crop on weedy land but were undertaken on the experimental station. The yields of sweet clover over a period of the last three years, averaged '51 of a ton per acre when sown with wheat and -91 of a ton when sown
alone. Over a period of eight years, sweet clover seeded with a nurse crop averaged -89 of a ton per acre. Over this same period brome grass averaged '79 of a ton and_ western rye an average of "97 of a ton per acre. Owing to dry weather the yields of sweet clover, brome or western rye have not been satisfactory at Swift Current.
2.	Brome grass and western rye grass stand the winter and dry weather better than other grasses in that district. Brome grass, however, is difficult to control. Arctic sweet clover seems to be the most hardy and most satisfactory.

speechtext:
Before this motion
passes, I think it is well to direct the attention of the house to the fact that it calls for a return of information relating to details in the operation of the Canadian farm loan board which has been established not as a department of the government, but as a separate organization in which the shareholders are the participating provincial governments and the Dominion government. The bulk of the capital requirements at the moment are provided, of course, by the federal treasury. The capital nonstock holders include the provincial governments and as well the borrowers under the statute, and the scheme contemplates eventually the sale of farm loan bonds to the public. Looking at the motion as it reads, it will be observed that this government is supposed to supply the particulars of the administration of a body which it does not control, and which exists by statute. These particulars we feel we should not be asked to supply at least before first consulting the participating provincial governments who are as much interested as we are. As will be recalled, the statute provides for an audit of the business of the board, which audit is carried on by the Auditor General. Under the circumstances I think that this is a motion that should not pass. It may stand if the hon. gentleman desires to look into it further, in which case it will go to the foot of the list. Otherwise I cannot think that it is sound to go into the details-we are not able to do it ourselves-of the business of an organization set up by statute in which, for the purpose of enabling it efficiently to function, we are shareholders.

speechtext:
Mr. O'SOAR L. BOULANGRR (Belle-chasse) moved:
That, in the opinion of this house, in order to relieve unemployment in the cities by encouraging a movement of return to the land, the government of Canada should invite railroads to reestablish reduced passenger rates in favour of colonists, and should by means of grants from public moneys help railroads to reestablish those rates, if necessary.
He said: I do not think it is necessary for me to take up very much of the time of the house to explain the resolution which Your Honour has just read. Its meaning is quite plain; the resolution speaks for itself. Rather, I shall take a few minutes to state my reasons for submitting this resolution to the kind consideration of the house.

Unemployment Relief
My only object in inviting discussion of the subject matter of the resolution is to offer a most humble suggestion for the relief of unemployment in the cities and to indicate one way of obtaining a better distribution of population in Canada, or in other words, a better equilibrium between the rural and the urban population.
Representing as I do an entirely rural county, the greater part of which has been settled for nearly three hundred years, and living in the nearby city of Quebec, I have observed many times in my own experience that the most difficult phase of the unemployment problem in the cities consists in providing relief and work for the surplus rural population which i3 attracted to the cities. In a county like the one which I have the honour to represent in this house, where every available place is filled, and where the land is already subdivided to excess, there is bound to be every year a surplus population since large families continue to be the general rule. Every year two or three hundred young farmers who cannot place themselves in their native parishes have to leave the county in order to seek their livelihood elsewhere. Where do they go? A few of them, the wise ones, faithful to the traditional calling of their class, and knowing that farming is the occupation in which, owing to their preparation, they have the greatest chance of succeeding, go on the land in the newer parts of the province of Quebec or in some other Canadian province. But the majority of them drift to the cities, to Quebec, which is only a few miles away from their homes, or to the great metropolis of Montreal, or to the industrial cities of New England, which are only a few hours distant. What chance of earning a decent living and of finding suitable employment have those country people, those farmers' sons in the city? They have no trade, they are unskilled labourers working by the day at casual jobs, never sure of steady employment for any length of time; they are unused to the city ways and to industrial life. When employment becomes at all scarce they are the first to suffer; they are the first recruits for the army of the unemployed and the first cases for relief by the charitable organizations or by the municipal, provincial or federal government. I think that this is a fair statement of the condition of the rural emigrants to the cities, and I venture to say that the majority of the unemployed who are to be found in our Canadian cities at the present time are former country people who abandoned their homes from one to five years ago.
What are the remedies for such a situation? There must be a few. For the moment I limit myself to suggesting one very respectfully to the government, and that is the inauguration of a back-to-the-land movement by requesting the Canadian railways to reestablish the homeseekers' excursions and the settlers' rates of a few years ago, and by assisting the railways to do so with government grants, if necessary.
In making this suggestion I am not unmindful of the present condition of agriculture. I do not forget that owing to the complete neglect of the farmers by the present government the prices of farm products are to-day the lowest they have been for twenty-five years, whereas the prices of the articles they have to buy have either gone up or have remained stationary when they should have gone down, as a result of the recent tariff manipulation. I am aware that farmers in some sections of the country do not want the competition of more farmers, that there is over-production in some branches of our agricultural activities, and that the sale of our farm products in foreign markets is jeopardized by the very peculiar attitude of this government in respect to international trade. But in spite of all these drawbacks I persist in my opinion that it would be to the advantage of Canada to assist in returning to the land the former rural people who glut the employment market of the cities. Even if these people could not get rich in producing and selling farm produce at present prices, they could at least eke out a living for themselves and their families on the farm. They could at least be sure of their bread, butter, milk, eggs, meat, fuel and so forth, instead of starving in the cities, where they have to pay for everything they need, including the water they drink.
The government, if they wanted to interest themselves in that class of needy Canadians for whom I speak, could supplement the back-to-the-land movement by assistance to farmers in the form of clearing premiums or first-ploughing premiums to be paid to farmers in certain definite sections of the country where the farms have not been developed sufficiently to support their owners adequately, and this could be done in co-operation with provincial governments, as outlined in my humible remarks during the debate on the address. The government could even study a plan of decentralization of industry whereby workers working on piece work or under some similar arrangement could be settled in villages not far from the plant, where they could own their cottage and plot of ground,
Unemployment Relief

raise their own vegetables, keep a cow, perhaps, a pig or two, and hens, and live cheaply and more happily than it is possible for them to do in the slums of the large city of Montreal, which have been so appallingly described by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). To my mind it is neither a normal nor a healthy condition of affairs that one-tenth of the population of Canada should be crowded into one city and one-third of the balance in the other Canadian cities. The adoption of the plan which I submit for the approval of the house would have a tendency, I believe, to remedy such a situation.
One objection which no doubt will be made to the adoption of the plan which I now have the honour of proposing is that the present financial condition of the Canadian railways might not permit the restoration of low rates for the transportation of settlers and their effects. If such is the case I hope the government will come to their rescue and will recoup them for the loss they would thus incur. I am sure that the government will not plead against the suggestion, the necessity for economy, because the money spent for the return to the land of the rurals presently unemployed in the cities would be money well spent. Probably it would relieve the government of the obligation of voting again next fall 820,000,000 for the assistance of the army of unskilled day labourers in the cities. In support of my contention that the government should assist the railways in inaugurating a back-to-the- land movement I wish to mention the precedent of the so-called assisted immigration which until very recently was practised, if it is not yet in vogue. The Canadian government did not refuse to assist the navigation and railway companies with money grants to enable them to bring immigrants from Europe to this country. The government each year spent considerable sums of money in caring for those immigrants after their arrival in Canada, and in helping them to make a beginning.
What the government did for strangers I hope they will gladly do for Canadians. If assisted immigration was good for Canada in the years of prosperity, and if the opposition blamed the then government for not promoting further immigration, the assistance of colonization by Canadians will be equally good. The obvious advantage of assisted colonization will be to improve the lot of a great number of Canadians who are now starving in the cities, to lessen unemployment, to obviate the necessity of voting another 820,000,000 for the relief of unem-

ployment and to increase the development of the country which, even in lean years, must go on. Therefore it is with great confidence that I submit for the approval of the house the resolution which was inspired by the above thoughts and which aims to effect their realization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes of the time of the house to discuss this proposal. The primary object of the motion before us is to redistribute to a substantial extent the population of Canada, and to place people on the land. The first reaction I had when I listened to the argument of my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) was that if agriculture were successful in this country there would be no need to reduce fares in order to get people on the land. In my judgment the condition of agriculture at the present time does not warrant this house or any other public body in spending one dollar to get one. more person back to the land. For many years I have objected to our immigration policy. On many occasions I have stated on the floor of the house that it would be far better for Canada to cancel its immigration policy and give our own Canadians an opportunity, if they so desire of going on the land. If I had any influence with the legislatures of the western provinces at the present time I would suggest to them that instead of opening up new areas for settlement those areas now not settled should be withdrawn. To-day in western Canada we have thousands and thousands of people who for the last twenty or thirty years have been living from twenty to sixty miles from railways. Our railways are not in a position to catch up with the requirements of those people or to provide them with reasonable transportation facilities. That being so why should we advocate a policy which would make worse a condition which already is bad. I have always objected to the plan of assisted immigration. In my judgment such a plan would not operate for the benefit of Canada. I objected even to the plan concerning the 3,000 British immigrants whereby the imperial government supplied those people with cash to pay their railway and boat fares, and an added sum with which they were to buy stock and implements in Canada. I have come across many cases where Canada has provided land at a reasonable valuation, and very few of those settlers have made good. My attitude towards the policy of immigration has been that which I am now describing. I have always felt we should first take care of our own

Unemployment Relief
people before we spend money to induce other people to enter Canada for the purpose of taking land.
In view of the. condition of agriculture and in so far as agricultural products are concerned at the present time I believe we would be well advised to give up any settlement policy until such time as consumption catches up with production. We should not adopt such a policy until the people now on the land are in a position to make a profit from their operations. These are my main objections to the motion now before the house, and I trust the government will not consider the possibility of asking the railways to reduce fares.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the two hon. gentlemen who have just addressed the house on this question have given to the house and the country the two different viewpoints involved. One has favoured the granting of special rates to those Canadians wishing to go back to the land, and the othei has taken the attitude that in view of present conditions such action would not be wise. Without in any way attempting to decide which of the two hon. members is right, may I point out that certainly the railways would be embarrassed if at this time they were asked to give special consideration in the way of passenger or freight rates. Continually they are being asked for reductions of the rates in both lines of traffic.
As far as the passenger rates are concerned, it might be well at this time to give some facts in connection with the Canadian National Railways; I have not the figures for the Canadian Pacific Railway. For some years passenger returns of the Canadian National Railways have been decreasing. Not long ago I had occasion to inquire from the officers of the railway company concerning the returns derived from passenger traffic during the past five years. I had expected to lea-m that the passenger returns were not increasing. To my horror however I learned that not only were passenger returns of the Canadian National not increasing but they were decreasing so rapidly that between the. years 1926 and 1930 the deficit had increased to a very startling extent. It has been the opinion of many that the various facilities being provided to accommodate the passenger traffic of both lines would increase the returns from that branch of the service. But, on the contrary, the passenger earnings of both railways have decreased to such an alarming extent that I do not think it would be fair to ask their respective managements to consider the adoption of the hon. member's proposal unless on
the understanding that they must be remunerated by some other agency for any losses that might thereby be sustained.
May I point out at this juncture that if the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway-I think we may take them together-are to be asked, as they are being asked continually, to reduce then passenger and freight rates, it seems to me that they should not be expected to absorb, on behalf of the country as a whole, such reductions in their earnings. I say this because from all over the country requests come to me as Minister of Railways asking for reductions in freight rates, for branch line construction, and for other expenditures which would mean a capital outlay of vast proportions. Perhaps it would interest the house to know that since we came into office eight or nine months ago I have had requests for branch lines, for stations, for hotels, for freight sheds, and so on, representing a capital investment on the part of the railway company of about 8200,000,000. I had the matter gone into some time ago because I wondered how much capital expenditure all these requests involved, and the itemized statements given to me show that total.

speechtext:
I cannot give my hon.
friend an intelligent answer offhand. But I may state this, I do not believe it is the duty of any government at this time to interfere in any way with the management of the national railways in their attempt to cut down unprofitable expenditures of this kind where it can be justified; it seems to me that it is our duty to give the national railways-and for that matter the Canadian Pacific company as well, because I also get protests

against proposed Canadian Pacific reductions in service-I say it is our duty to give them at least a fighting chance to make ends meet when they can show that these reductions in service will result in substantial economies. Individual sections of the country directly affected will of course protest, and naturally I have to pass on the protests to the railways. But the management of both railway systems must be permitted to reduce their operating losses so far as government, and for that matter parliament too, can permit them so to do.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext: Does not the railway commission have some control over the railways?

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
Entirely. I do not mean
to suggest that the government has any control in this respect. My right hon. friend is quite right, the railway commission has control, and if the local authorities affected protest to the commission, and can prove that the proposed reductions are unjustified, no doubt the commission will heed their protests. But it is not the part of government or parliament, for political or other reasons, to override the decisions of the railway companies^ in matters such as this, particularly when it is remembered that, as shown by the report recently tabled, the Canadian National Railway system's earnings are insufficient by nearly $30,000,000 to meet the interest on its public indebtedness to say nothing of the interest owing to the Dominion government for the hundreds of millions invested in the system; and it is unable to pay for the additions and betterments of various kinds which have been outlined. I say that when the system is unable to meet these obligations, it is the duty of government, parliament and people, so far as they can, to cooperate in encouraging reductions in operating expenses. Not only should the Canadian National Railways management be encouraged, but the Canadian Pacific Railway management as well, in their efforts to bring their revenues to the point where they will meet their expenditures. I mention that last matter because I thought it was a good opportunity to bring this question before the public in general in order that the public might understand that, as the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) pointed out, this is a matter for the railway commission to deal with if any locality is being unjustly treated, as sometimes may occur.
Having pointed out these facts; having shown the necessity for the railways being

Unemployment Relief
given an opportunity to carry on in order to earn revenues that will come somewhere near covering their expenses, I may say to my hon. friend who very fairly proposed the motion (Mr. Boulanger) that I certainly will see that it reaches the managements of the two railways for whatever consideration they may choose to give it. I shall gladly do that for him. Having said that, and the motion haying been made in the house, perhaps he will feel that he has accomplished the desired purpose in bringing the matter before the government and the railways. He might feel that it has been satisfactorily concluded, and withdraw his motion.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext: Before the minister concludes, may I ask if it is not a fact that within the last week or two reduced passenger rates have been put into effect by the railways?

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
Yes, my right hon. friend
is quite correct. Within the last week or two the railways have reduced the week end fares quite materially. I presume that has been done in order to encourage more passenger traffic than they are getting at present, due to the interference with that traffic of motor buses and private motor cars. I know, from the reports not only of our own railway but also of the Canadian Pacific Railway^ and American roads, that the inroads into railway revenues because of these private means of locomotion are so severe that the railways all over the world are feeling the situation very severely. These reduced rates, to which my right hon. friend referred, are for week end trips all over the country, in an endeavour to pick up a certain amount of the traffic which has been lost. I do not know of any other reductions which have been made.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
Does the minister regard it
as possible, in the interests of the country and of the revenues of the railways, to suggest to the executives of the two roads that they cooperate with a view to cutting out duplication of services?

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
I may answer that by saying that this suggestion already has been made to the railways. As my hon. friend knows, it has been made numbers of times through the press; I presume it was made by the late government, although I do not know anything about that, and the present government has suggested to the railways that duplication should be ended.
In that regard I may say that I have discussed the question with the heads of both railways, and it seems a particularly difficult
matter for them to decide upon. Naturally the railroad, whichever it may be, which carries the greater proportion of passenger traffic on a certain train does not care to give up that traffic. In another case perhaps the other line has an advantage and does not wish to give it up. From my conversations with the heads of the railways it seems a very difficult question indeed to come to an agreement upon, though both Mr. Beatty and Sir Henry Thornton have expressed publicly, and to myself privately, the desire to do away with unnecessary duplication. I might say to my hon. friend that I believe the heavy decrease in earnings will make it necessary for the railways to come to some decision in that regard in the near future.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext: My thought was that perhaps the genial minister himself, with his faculty of getting people together, might have considerable success if he took more interest in pushing that suggestion.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
I believe I mentioned
that the suggestion has been made by the government since we came into office. It was made by myself verbally and it has been made by my right hon. leader more than once.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
The minister indicated
that he was willing to submit this motion to the railway companies. I presume he means only the first part of the motion; I suppose there would be no indication of an intention on the part of the government to make up any possible difference from public moneys.
I think I understood that quite clearly from the remarks of the minister.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
I meant, of course, that
I would submit the first part of the motion to the companies. With regard to the government helping out, unfortunately that is being done very largely now through the heavy charges upon the government in connection with deficits and for capital advances which are necessary in regard to the national railway. Unfortunately, as I have said, the national railways are not earning enough to pay for their own capital advances, so I suppose indirectly the government pays very heavily towards such traffic of that kind as already goes on. The question of going further in that direction would be a matter of government policy, which I should not care to discuss on a motion of this kind. I might say that it would be given consideration; I suppose that is the ordinary phrase.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house and
Unemployment Relief

the country will agree with the statement of the Minister of Railways, looking at it from the point of view of the transportation companies. In my own riding I have some branch lines which have been operating for fifteen or sixteen years. They started with a daily service but after fifteen years, in spite of all the development that has taken place, we now find the railway companies proposing to give us a tri-weekly service. I have made representations in the interests of those people, to see if it is not possible to continue the daily service. The people there cannot see the necessity for this reduction in service. If it was necessary fifteen years ago, when the tonnage amounted to a certain figure, to carry on a daily service, now when the tonnage must be vastly greater they do not see why they should have to submit to a tri-weekly service.
That is looking at the matter from a freight standpoint, but there are other considerations. There is the question of train service in the winter time, and there is the question of mail. The people of western Canada go into the larger centres for hospital accommodation. They will find it very difficult to carry on with a reduced service, and it would be hard for anyone to convince these people that the railway companies should be allowed at this time to reduce the service.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
I know I am out of order in continuing the debate, but the whole discussion has been out of order in its latter stages. However, perhaps I might say that no matter how we feel in the matter, the government has not the power to interfere. This is a matter for the railway commission, and while naturally anyone who has lived in pioneer sections of the country, as I did during many of my early years, realizes the feelings^ of a group of people who are being partly isolated through tri-weekly service, at the same time one cannot help but have sympathy for the railways which are trying to cut down some of their unnecessary expenses.
I find	in	my	pocket, although	I did notbring it	for	the	purposes of this	discussion,
a report covering one section of the country'
I	will not say which section; it will be either
the east or the west, as my hon. friend expressed it, but I will not say which. This is a report	of	the	national railways	in regardto some	of	the	reductions which	they are
making. They state for example that on one line their revenue at the present time is
II	cents per train mile, while the cost to them is 97i cents. We cannot blame them for

trying to reduce that loss, which is more or less unavoidable. In the next case they cite, the revenue per train mile is 37 cents and the cost 97J cents, and in another instance the revenue is 15 cents per train mile as compared with a cost of 98i cents. Going further down the list, I find that in another instance the revenue is given as 11 cents per train mile while the cost is 74 cents. And taking one more example-the worst in the way of considerable loss-the revenue is 13 cents as against a cost of 126-2 cents. In other words, the cost is nearly ten times as much as the revenue. Yet only yesterday there came to mv office a deputation from the section affected by that last figure I gave. They pointed out that there were 32,000 people on that section of the line who were being served by this particular branch line, and that they were engaged in a certain form of business which they were afraid would be ruined by the cut-off of the train, notwithstanding, as I have stated, that the cost to the railway is ten times the earnings received on this branch. No one can blame the railway for endeavouring to reduce the loss, nor can anyone very well quarrel with the people in the section concerned. I suggest that, in such a case as this, or in the case of my hon. friend's section, if the people affected feel that there is an injustice the only body that can really interfere in the matter is the Board of Railway Commissioners. I fear that this is the policy which will be adhered to, and I suggest that any section that feels it is being unfairly treated will have to make its representations to the Board of Railway Commissioners, who I have no doubt will prevent the railway from discontinuing the service if such discontinuance is not justified. That is one of the functions of the board.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext: Following up what the minister has said, I would ask this question. Supposing the railways should institute a triweekly instead of a daily service: we all know it is much easier to lose something than to get it back. When we lose this service, is there any understanding between the Board of Railway Commissioners and the railways that, when the tonnage or the occasion permits, it will be just as easy for us to get that service back as it had been to lose it? Perhaps I should not ask the minister that question.

There is no doubt that if the traffic on that section of the line increases, the railway affected will resume the service. The cut-off of the service is but for a period, for this year, without any intention of con-

I am sure that if either of the railways can be shown that traffic anj -where is not being properly taken care of, and if they can approximately pay their way, they will be only too glad to resume the service.

Will the minister permit
one other question? I should be glad if he would indicate in a general way what the policy of the transportation companies is as regards going into the bus or truck service It would seem, from what the minister has said, that the buses or trucks have an advantage in the short haul, and that the railway companies have to concentrate on the long-haul business to make their revenue. It sometimes happens, when the roads are good, that service can be provided by the buses and trucks; but when the roads are impassable, of course that service cannot be carried on, and merchants have great difficulty in getting their supplies, while passengers are unable to reach their destination. It has occurred to me that if there were some form of combined service or some cooperation between the railway companies and the buses, probably service might be rendered. Are the transportation companies considering these other methods of dealing with the problem?

The house not being in
committee, each hon. member has the right to make only one speech. I think we had better adhere to the rules.

subtopic: MOTION TO REDUCE RAILWAY PASSENGER RATES FOR COLONISTS
speechtext:
It seems to me that we have got
away from the resolution, which, as I read it, is a contribution towards the relief of unemployment. The hon. member who moved the motion put up what I regard as a good argument. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) objected to that policy on the ground that there were too many people on the land at the present time. The Minister of Railways, however, presented a different argument on behalf of the railway companies
_that they ought not to be expected to take
any lower compensation than they are receiving at the present time. I do not see anything here that would in any way reduce the earning power of the railway companies; the resolution provides for grants from public moneys to make up any deficiency which the railways might suffer. I understood that the Conservatives, at their convention in Winnipeg in 1927,
indicated in their platform that they would give special consideration and offer special privileges to anyone who wanted to settle on the land. As I understood the Minister of Railways, what he advocated would mean greater unemployment rather than the relief of the present situation, inasmuch as-if I rightly, understand him-he has been discussing with the railway companies the advisability of taking off more trains, or eliminating the duplication of trains. Every railway tram you take off adds five more men to the number of unemployed, and every time you reduce a train service it similarly increases unemployment. There is, therefore, probably a great deal to be said for the resolution. If we are going to encourage people to settle on the land, if we are going to encourage citizens from other parts of the country to take up land, and if at the same time we do not want to impair the railway earnings, then we should be prepared to act in accordance with the Conservative platform of the Winnipeg convention-reimburse the railway companies from the public funds.

Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford): Just a word or two. While I have had no complaints from my own constituency in regard to the reduction or the elimination of railway services, I might say that since this question is, properly speaking, quite a national one at the present time, there is one point which I think might be impressed upon the Minister of Railways. It is this. Sometimes when railway services are eliminated or reduced the feeling in the community affected is that the elimination or reduction is made not on the basis of earnings but by reason of the fact that other lines are not paying. I would urge upon the minister that whenever any service is either discontinued or reduced he do his best to see that such elimination or reduction is based absolutely on the exigencies of the line in question and not on conditions existing in some other section of the railway.
